name: Stock split
title: Stock split: Formula, Example & Limits
description: A stock split proportionally changes a company’s share count and corresponding per-share amounts.
definition: A stock split proportionally changes a company’s share count and corresponding per-share amounts. A forward split increases theoretical shares; a reverse split reduces them according to the stated new-for-old ratio.
explanation: For an intact position, multiply share quantity by the ratio and divide reference price and average acquisition cost per share by it. The proportional action alone preserves reference holding value and entered total cost.
formula: Factor = new shares / old shares; quantity after = quantity before × factor; reference price and average cost per share divide by factor
formulaNote: Manual proportional changes to an intact position. Theoretical fractional shares are retained. No cash-in-lieu, broker rounding, market quotation, lot-level tax reporting, sale or corporate-action eligibility is inferred.

example.title: A 3-for-2 split turns 120 shares into 180 theoretical shares
example.intro: 120 shares before the split; $45 reference market price; $30 average acquisition cost per share; 3 new shares for every 2 old shares.
steps: The new-for-old factor is 3 / 2 = 1.5. Multiply share quantity by that factor.
Divide the reference price by 1.5 to get $30 and average acquisition cost by 1.5 to get $20 per share.
Check the totals: 180 × $30 remains $5,400 of reference value; 180 × $20 remains $3,600 of acquisition cost.
example.answer: The theoretical holding is 180 shares. The proportional split alone creates no gain in total reference value.
example.assumptions: Manual proportional changes to an intact position. Theoretical fractional shares are retained. No cash-in-lieu, broker rounding, market quotation, lot-level tax reporting, sale or corporate-action eligibility is inferred.

pitfall.title: More shares alone do not create an investment gain
pitfall.text: Actual market prices can change, and fractional-share settlement depends on issuer and broker terms. A proportional reference price is not a market prediction.

tools.text: Reconcile theoretical shares, proportional reference price and preserved total cost.
Reconcile purchase quantities and entered costs to an average acquisition amount.

scope: Manual proportional changes to an intact position. Theoretical fractional shares are retained. No cash-in-lieu, broker rounding, market quotation, lot-level tax reporting, sale or corporate-action eligibility is inferred.

name: Customer acquisition cost
title: Customer acquisition cost: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Customer acquisition cost is the included cost of an acquisition effort divided by unique new customers in the same defined scope.
definition: Customer acquisition cost is the included cost of an acquisition effort divided by unique new customers in the same defined scope. The time window, customer definition and cost allocation are essential parts of the measure.
explanation: A customer should be counted once when first acquired. Advertising, allocated personnel, agency, software and other acquisition items must not overlap. ROAS instead compares attributed revenue with advertising spend.
formula: CAC = nonoverlapping acquisition costs / unique new customers in the matching period and scope
formulaNote: Manual costs and unique-new-customer counts for a user-defined matching scope. No CRM connection, automatic attribution, customer lifetime value, universal good-CAC threshold or budget recommendation.

example.title: Reconcile $25,000 of acquisition costs for 100 new customers
example.intro: One selected acquisition cohort and reporting window: 100 unique new customers; $12,000 advertising; $8,000 allocated acquisition personnel; $5,000 other acquisition costs; no separate agency or software costs.
steps: Reconcile nonoverlapping costs: $12,000 + $8,000 + $5,000 = $25,000. The personnel and other amounts must not already be included in advertising.
Divide the selected total by 100 unique new customers. Count each newly acquired customer once, even if that customer places multiple orders.
Record whether the window describes a campaign, channel or company-wide cohort so a later comparison uses the same scope.
example.answer: CAC is $250 per new customer for this defined cost scope. That amount alone does not establish profit or an acceptable advertising budget.
example.assumptions: Manual costs and unique-new-customer counts for a user-defined matching scope. No CRM connection, automatic attribution, customer lifetime value, universal good-CAC threshold or budget recommendation.

expected.label: Acquisition cost per unique new customer

pitfall.title: Orders and leads are different denominators
pitfall.text: Replacing unique new customers with repeat orders, visits or leads produces another metric. State the customer and cost definitions beside the result.

tools.text: Match nonoverlapping acquisition costs with unique new customers.
Express attributed revenue per advertising dollar rather than cost per new customer.

scope: Manual costs and unique-new-customer counts for a user-defined matching scope. No CRM connection, automatic attribution, customer lifetime value, universal good-CAC threshold or budget recommendation.

name: Dividend discount model
title: Dividend discount model: Formula, Example & Limits
description: A dividend discount model estimates equity value as the present value of assumed future dividends.
definition: A dividend discount model estimates equity value as the present value of assumed future dividends. The stable-growth Gordon form divides the next annual dividend by required return minus perpetual growth.
explanation: The latest dividend D0 must first grow to the next dividend D1 when that is the input convention. Required return must exceed perpetual growth in the modeled stable stage. A two-stage model discounts early dividends and a later terminal value separately.
formula: Stable value = D1 / (r − g); two-stage value = PV of early dividends + PV of terminal price at year N
formulaNote: Manual annual end-period dividend assumptions and one annual required equity return. Stable-stage return must exceed growth. No dividend lookup, trading recommendation, automatic growth forecast or tax calculation.

example.title: Grow the latest $2 dividend before applying Gordon growth
example.intro: Latest annual dividend D0 $2 per share; perpetual growth 4%; required annual return 10%.
steps: Calculate the next annual dividend: D1 = $2 × 1.04 = $2.08.
Divide D1 by the rate spread: $2.08 / (0.10 − 0.04). Using D0 directly would miss one growth step.
The perpetual-growth assumption requires the required return to exceed growth. Small changes in that spread can greatly change value.
example.answer: The assumed dividend stream has a modeled value of about $34.67 per share; this is not a market quote or guaranteed return.
example.assumptions: Manual annual end-period dividend assumptions and one annual required equity return. Stable-stage return must exceed growth. No dividend lookup, trading recommendation, automatic growth forecast or tax calculation.

pitfall.title: A model value is not a promised trading price
pitfall.text: Small assumption changes can produce large valuation changes. DDM does not predict dividend policy, reinvestment prices or realized investment returns.

tools.text: Test the present value of an assumed dividend stream and rate spread.
Explore a dividend-reinvestment accumulation path rather than a present-value stock valuation.

scope: Manual annual end-period dividend assumptions and one annual required equity return. Stable-stage return must exceed growth. No dividend lookup, trading recommendation, automatic growth forecast or tax calculation.

name: Earnings per share
title: Earnings per share: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Basic earnings per share is period earnings available to common shareholders divided by weighted average common shares for that period.
definition: Basic earnings per share is period earnings available to common shareholders divided by weighted average common shares for that period. It is a profit-per-share accounting measure.
explanation: An applicable preferred earnings adjustment is separate from ordinary common dividends. Share issuances and other changes require appropriate time weighting and any needed restatement. Diluted EPS addresses potential common shares using additional rules.
formula: Basic EPS = (net income − entered preferred earnings adjustment) / weighted average common shares
formulaNote: A simplified basic-EPS worksheet using an already-checked preferred earnings adjustment and a supplied average or complete share/day schedule. No automatic diluted EPS, corporate-action restatement or complete reporting compliance.

example.title: Allocate $900,000 of common earnings over 300,000 average shares
example.intro: $1,000,000 period net income; $100,000 entered preferred earnings adjustment; 300,000 weighted average common shares.
steps: Subtract the applicable preferred earnings adjustment: $1,000,000 − $100,000 = $900,000.
Divide common earnings by weighted average common shares for that same period. The adjustment must match the accounting treatment being analyzed.
example.answer: Basic EPS is $3 per common share. It does not include option, convertible-security or other diluted-EPS adjustments.
example.assumptions: A simplified basic-EPS worksheet using an already-checked preferred earnings adjustment and a supplied average or complete share/day schedule. No automatic diluted EPS, corporate-action restatement or complete reporting compliance.

pitfall.title: An ending share count is not automatically the period average
pitfall.text: A denominator that ignores timing can distort basic EPS. Adding arbitrary shares does not automatically create a valid diluted result.

tools.text: Reconcile common earnings and weighted common shares for basic EPS.
Compare period accounting earnings with average book equity.

scope: A simplified basic-EPS worksheet using an already-checked preferred earnings adjustment and a supplied average or complete share/day schedule. No automatic diluted EPS, corporate-action restatement or complete reporting compliance.

name: Sharpe ratio
title: Sharpe ratio: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Sharpe ratio compares arithmetic mean excess return with the standard deviation of those excess returns over a matching observation period.
definition: Sharpe ratio compares arithmetic mean excess return with the standard deviation of those excess returns over a matching observation period. It is dimensionless, rather than a percentage return.
explanation: The benchmark and return period must match. This worksheet’s sequence mode uses sample standard deviation and a constant same-period risk-free return. Optional square-root annualization relies on assumptions rather than supplying an exact compounded return.
formula: Period Sharpe = mean(excess return) / standard deviation(excess return); assumed annual Sharpe = period Sharpe × sqrt(periods per year)
formulaNote: Manual equally spaced simple returns or matched statistics. Series mode uses sample standard deviation (n−1), a fixed same-period risk-free return and an explicit annualization count. No market-price feed, portfolio optimization or performance guarantee.

example.title: An 8-percentage-point annual excess return over 16% volatility
example.intro: Annual arithmetic mean return 12%; annual risk-free return 4%; annual excess-return standard deviation 16%; one observation period per year.
steps: Subtract the matching-period risk-free return: 12% − 4% = 8 percentage points.
Divide 8 by 16. Because the statistics are already annual and the scaling factor is one, no monthly-to-annual conversion is applied.
example.answer: The Sharpe ratio is 0.5, a dimensionless ratio rather than a 0.5% return or a guarantee of future performance.
example.assumptions: Manual equally spaced simple returns or matched statistics. Series mode uses sample standard deviation (n−1), a fixed same-period risk-free return and an explicit annualization count. No market-price feed, portfolio optimization or performance guarantee.

expected.label: Sharpe ratio for one observation period

pitfall.title: A Sharpe ratio is not CAGR or total profit
pitfall.text: A short sample, autocorrelation or very low volatility can make the ratio unstable. Zero volatility leaves it undefined; negative excess return can produce a negative ratio.

tools.text: Inspect matching-period excess returns, sample volatility and annualization assumptions.
Examine return and cash-flow timing separately from a volatility-normalized score.

sources.title: William F. Sharpe: The Sharpe Ratio

scope: Manual equally spaced simple returns or matched statistics. Series mode uses sample standard deviation (n−1), a fixed same-period risk-free return and an explicit annualization count. No market-price feed, portfolio optimization or performance guarantee.

name: Black-Scholes-Merton model
title: Black-Scholes-Merton model: Formula, Example & Limits
description: The Black–Scholes–Merton model estimates theoretical European option values from spot, strike, time, annual volatility and consistent interest and dividend-rate assumptions.
definition: The Black–Scholes–Merton model estimates theoretical European option values from spot, strike, time, annual volatility and consistent interest and dividend-rate assumptions.
explanation: This worksheet uses continuously compounded annual rates and a continuous dividend yield. It returns model values per share. At zero remaining time, the modeled value becomes the corresponding intrinsic payoff.
formula: C = S exp(−qT)N(d1) − K exp(−rT)N(d2); C − P = S exp(−qT) − K exp(−rT)
formulaNote: European exercise with constant annual volatility and continuous rates. Per-share theory values only; no American early exercise, discrete cash dividends, real-time quotes, implied-volatility estimation or employee-option accounting determination.

example.title: Price a one-year European call with $100 spot and strike
example.intro: Spot $100; strike $100; one year to expiry; 20% annual volatility; 5% continuously compounded risk-free rate; zero continuous dividend yield.
steps: Use rates as decimals and time in years. The normal-distribution inputs are d1 = 0.35 and d2 = 0.15.
Evaluate S × N(d1) − K × exp(−rT) × N(d2) under the zero-dividend assumptions.
The result is a theoretical value per share. A contract multiplier, actual premium paid, fees and early exercise are separate questions.
example.answer: The European call’s modeled value is about $10.450584 per share. It is neither an expiration profit nor a live option quote.
example.assumptions: European exercise with constant annual volatility and continuous rates. Per-share theory values only; no American early exercise, discrete cash dividends, real-time quotes, implied-volatility estimation or employee-option accounting determination.

expected.label: European call theoretical value per share

pitfall.title: Theoretical value is not a trade profit or execution quote
pitfall.text: An actual trade needs its premium, fees, contract terms and outcome. European-model values do not automatically handle American early exercise or dated cash dividends.
